name: Dashboard
description: The screen a user lands on after signing in: a strip of figures, one plot, and the queues that are actually waiting for them. Every part of it already exists — this entry is the composition and the rules that govern it.
when_to_use: The first screen after sign-in, and the only screen in the application whose job is to be left. It exists for orientation and triage — what changed since yesterday, what is on fire, what is waiting on you — and it is finished the moment somebody clicks out of it into the record they came to work on. It is not for analysis. A screen with one question rather than eight is a chart in a card with the figures under it and no strip above it, and the moment somebody wants to sort by vendor, narrow to a plant and work down the result, they want index-page, which is where the strip and every queue on this page link to. Reach for list-detail instead when the queue is the whole day's work and each record is decided and left behind — a QC hold run, an approval run of forty — because that layout keeps the queue on screen and this one hands it away on the first click. The test is whether anybody has ever done a second thing here without navigating: if they have, the screen is a register with figures over it and it belongs in index-page. A dashboard that shows a buyer four charts and no list of what needs approving today has failed at this component's job whatever else it does.
rules: The page renders inside app-shell, in <main>, like every other signed-in screen. The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page, drop the wrapper's height and border and keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter, which is the one app-shell's own main column already uses.

The order of the regions is the component. Figures, then the queues, then the plot. Put the plots second and on a 1280px laptop the list of what needs approving today lands below the fold, so the buyer scrolls past four charts every morning to reach the nine records that are the reason they opened the page — and after a fortnight they stop opening it and work out of the register instead. Nothing on a dashboard is ranked by how much room it takes; it is ranked by whether somebody has to act on it today.

Four figures is the ceiling on the strip, and it is a ceiling on meaning rather than on width. Everything on a dashboard is somebody's most important number, so a strip of four becomes a strip of seven without anyone deciding to, and at seven nobody reads any of them. The fifth metric is a request to demote one of the first four. This is stat-card's rule and it is restated here because the strip is where the pressure lands.

The greeting is not the h1. A heading outline whose top entry is "Good morning, Akshay" is identical on every dashboard the application will ever have and says nothing about which of eleven screens somebody is on. The greeting is a line above the title, the h1 names the desk, and the line under it carries the scope and the time the figures were read.

The as-of time is written once, on the page head, and never on the tiles. Four copies of 09:12 is four chances for the strip to disagree with itself, and the scope — three plants, one shift, this cost centre — is the same for every figure on the page. A figure nobody can reconcile against the register gets reconciled by hand exactly once, disagrees by a lakh, and is never trusted again.

A queue is a card with a count in its header, at most five rows, and a link to the register that holds the rest. Five is where a list stops being read at a glance and starts being a register drawn without a header; the sixth row is a request for index-page. Every row is a real link into a record, using table/linked-rows' stretched anchor, so the whole row is the target and the URL is copyable, openable in a tab and reachable by middle click.

The queue header link says how many and what they are. "All 9" is nine of what — the visible text carries the count and sr-only text finishes the sentence, because a dashboard with four queues is otherwise four links called All in the tab order.

A page made of regions that each load separately must reserve their heights before any of them answer. Every region has a known shape before it has data — a strip of four tiles, a five-row queue, a plot box of h-64 — so each one waits as a skeleton at its own measurements rather than as a spinner in a collapsed box. Eight regions resolving one at a time into boxes that grow on arrival walks the whole page up and down eight times, and the click somebody aimed at an approval lands on the row below it.

A region's retry targets the region, never the page. Inside a composed screen there is exactly one data-kui and it is the dashboard's, so chart/failed's hx-target="closest [data-kui]" swaps the entire dashboard out on a chart that did not answer — including the three regions that did. Give every independently-loading region an id and target that.

Write real hx-* attributes on the regions. htmx never processes hx-* that Alpine created after load, so a bound :hx-get inside an x-for is silently inert; a region that loads itself does it with hx-get and hx-trigger="load" written into the markup.

A period control rebases the figures and the plot and must not touch the queues. "Waiting on your approval" has no period — it is what is true now — and a control that appears to scope the whole page while three of its regions ignore it is worse than no control at all. Put the period over the regions it governs and say in the card what it governs.

Rebasing moves the figure, the magnitude of the delta and the clause naming what the delta is measured against, together, from one record. Move the figure and leave the clause and the page is not stale, it is false: "1,712 vs. July" is a sentence nobody catches because both halves look like data.

A second role is a second page, not the first page with things hidden. A storekeeper's dashboard has different figures, different queues and different links, and the buyer's committed-value plot is absent rather than empty — a storekeeper has no committed-value trend to read and never will. Rendering one page and hiding half of it leaves every hidden region in the DOM, in the tab order on the day somebody gets the class wrong, and it makes the storekeeper's screen a worse version of somebody else's instead of their own.

The exceptions band sits above the figures and is capped at three. Something earns a place there when it is actionable by this person today, time-bound, and not already counted in the strip; a fourth exception is a queue and belongs in a card with a count and a link. Nothing in the band dismisses, because dismissing it does not fix the record and it is back tomorrow — the way to clear an exception is to work it.

The band is alert's shape and it is neutral. White card, zinc border, colour only in the icon. A full-width red field across the top of a dashboard shouts louder than the twelve genuinely overdue orders it is describing, and the moment one region is red the graphite ones read as switched off.

Zero, nothing yet and could not read are three different tiles and a dashboard draws all three in its first week. Zero GRNs posted is a fact and renders as 0. A metric that does not exist yet renders as an em dash with one line saying when it starts. A read that failed renders as an em dash with a reason and a retry, and never as a zero — somebody sees zero QC holds, stops checking, and the line runs a shift on material that was never released.

A first-week dashboard is not empty-state/all-clear. Nothing has been cleared; nothing has happened. All-clear is the reward for emptying a queue and printing it over a queue that has never held anything is the one empty state that reads as a lie.

At 390px the strip and the plot both become a different thing rather than a narrower one, and neither is invented here: the four tiles become stat-card/dense — one card, four cells, two across — and the twelve-month plot keeps its box and drops labels through chart/responsive's autoSkip rather than rotating or abbreviating them. What this entry decides is which of those the dashboard picks and in what order the regions come, which is queues before plot at every width.

The dashboard takes page-header's title and meta without its white band. A dashboard has no record, no status pill and usually no primary action, so a full-bleed band across the column draws a rule under a title and nothing else. Where one does carry an action — New purchase order on a buyer's screen — it is page-header/default unchanged, band and all.

anatomy.description: The greeting line, the one h1 naming the desk, and the line under it carrying the scope and the as-of time. page-header's title block without its band.
Optional, above the figures, at most three alert cards. Actionable today, time-bound, not already counted in the strip, and never dismissible.
stat-card's grid — grid-cols-1, sm:grid-cols-2, xl:grid-cols-4, gap-3 — holding at most four tiles, each an anchor to the register behind its number.
A card: header with the count and a link to the register, then at most five rows, each a stretched anchor into one record. The working half of the page and the half that decides whether it gets used.
The count as visible text with sr-only words finishing the sentence, so four queues are not four links called All.
One chart, last, in a card of its own. It reads its colours out of the legend the way chart requires; the legend is markup, so it is present in every state the card can be in.
Any of the above as an independently-loaded block: its own id, its own hx-get, its own skeleton at its own measurements, and its own retry targeting that id.
button-group/segmented in the header of the region it governs, never floating over a page whose queues ignore it.
The line under the plot naming the source and the period. A figure with no stated period is a figure nobody can check.

behaviour: Every tile and every queue row navigates. There is no state on this page worth keeping, so nothing is worked in place and nothing is edited here.
Regions resolve independently and in any order. Each holds its own height from first paint, so the page does not move as they land and a click aimed at a row lands on that row.
A region that failed keeps the page. Its retry swaps that region by id and a second failure lands back in the same box rather than replacing a working dashboard with an error screen.
Changing the period rebases the figures, their deltas and the comparison clauses, and mutates the existing chart with update(). The queues do not move, because a queue has no period.
The new figure for a period is read for that period and never divided out of the one already on screen. 148 orders in thirty days does not become 34.5 in a week.
The exceptions band appears only when there is something in it. An empty band is a heading over nothing and teaches people to stop looking at that part of the screen.

A queue that empties draws empty-state/all-clear with the evidence in it — how many were cleared and by when — and only when no filter is in force. A queue that has never held anything draws nothing-yet instead.
Below sm the strip restacks and the queues become one column in DOM order, queues before plot. Nothing scrolls sideways at 390px.

The plot thins its axis as its box narrows and thickens it again when the box widens, which also covers the sidebar expanding and the card moving from a three-column grid to one — neither of which is a window resize.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, and the h1 names the screen rather than greeting the user. Every region below it is an h2 and anything inside a region is an h3.

Each region is a <section> with an accessible name, which makes it a landmark. On a dashboard that is the point: the landmark list is how somebody skips past four figures and a plot to the queue they came for, and it is the only navigation this page has.
The figure strip's heading is sr-only where the page head has already named the scope. A named region with no visible heading still needs a real heading element for the outline to hang off.

Each tile is a dt and dd pair inside a dl, so the label and the figure are one unit in the accessibility tree. The delta arrow is aria-hidden and the sign is real text, so the tile still reads with the icon and the colour both gone.

A queue row is one stretched anchor whose accessible name is the row — the document number, the vendor and the figure — and nothing else in the row is focusable, so Tab walks a queue one record at a time.
The queue header link carries its count as text and finishes its sentence with sr-only words naming the queue, because a dashboard of four queues is otherwise four adjacent links called All.
A loading region carries aria-busy and one sr-only role="status" naming what is coming. Its grey blocks are aria-hidden: eight rectangles announced one at a time is noise standing in for a wait.

The period control is a radiogroup and its aria-checked is the announcement. There is no live region over the strip. stat-card/period is right to make one tile a role="status" with aria-atomic, and it is wrong for a page of them — four figures, four comparison clauses and a chart summary read out on every press is a control nobody uses twice.

A failed region says so as ordinary text in the region. No role="alert" in static markup: it fires on first paint whether or not anything just went wrong, and the swap that put the region there is what announces.

A no-data figure spells out "No data" as sr-only text beside the aria-hidden em dash, and a failed one says "Not read". An em dash resolves to nothing, and a silent tile is indistinguishable from a missing one.

The plot canvas is role="img" with a sentence naming the shape, and it repeats its numbers as an sr-only table. A canvas has no text in it, so without one of the two a screen reader gets nothing at all.
Focus is an outline and never a ring, on the tiles, the queue rows and the retries alike. A ring compiles to a box-shadow and forced-colours mode drops every box-shadow.
